traveler: Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir
title: One Is Not Born: Montparnasse, the Agregation, and the Woman One Becomes
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Boulevard du Montparnasse, the birth of a first daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date 9 January 1908 given by English and French Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The address, 103 Boulevard du Montparnasse, and the description of the apartment come from French Wikipedia; the coordinates are a placement on that block, not a surveyed doorway
stops.campa: On the ninth of January, in a well-appointed and sparsely furnished apartment at 103 Boulevard du Montparnasse, Georges de Beauvoir and Francoise Brasseur have a first daughter and name her Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand. The father is a lawyer's son with a taste for amateur theatre and no religion of any kind. The mother is a devout Catholic out of Verdun, and it is her faith, not his want of one, that the daughters are raised inside. Two years later a second daughter, Helene, arrives and is called Poupette for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The apartment block at 103 Boulevard du Montparnasse, sixth arrondissement, birthplace
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Cours Desir, the Catholic schoolroom and Zaza
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The school, the Institut Adeline Desir known as the Cours Desir, is independently confirmed, but no precise street number was reachable, so the coordinates are approximate to the Saint-Germain quarter. She attends from early childhood to the baccalaureat, roughly 1913 to 1925; the month and day here are an ordering device only
stops.campa: She is sent young to the Institut Adeline Desir, a strict Catholic school for girls of good family in the Saint-Germain quarter, where the curriculum is piety and deportment and cleverness in a pupil is treated as a symptom. Here she meets Elisabeth Lacoin, called Zaza, and loves her past all measure; she writes afterwards that she loved no one in the world more. The two girls read together and argue theology, and plan lives their families have no intention of permitting. Their letters to each other survive, and are published long afterwards as Zaza: correspondance et carnets.
suggested_refs: The Institut Adeline Desir, the Cours Desir of the memoirs, Saint-Germain-des-Pres

stops.name: Rue de Rennes, the fall and the loss of God
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the move and the loss of fortune after the First World War, per English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The rejection of Catholicism at around fourteen is a reconstruction from the memoirs, tagged R by the Stanford entry, so the two events are placed at one address for narrative order. Coordinates are Nominatim's for 71 rue de Rennes; the street number itself is not stated in the fetched articles, only the street and the fifth-floor walk-up
stops.campa: The war ends and the family money is gone. The Beauvoirs move to a fifth-floor walk-up on the rue de Rennes with no elevator, no central heating, no running water and no bathroom; her mother carries the water up. Simone watches her father's contempt for a wife who has become poor, and understands early what a dowryless girl of her class is worth on the market she was raised for. The two facts, the poverty and the contempt, arrive in the same year and afterwards sit inside her as one fact. Somewhere around fourteen she stops believing in God. She tells nobody in the apartment.
stops.quote: Faith allows an evasion of those difficulties which the atheist confronts honestly.
stops.quote_source: All Said and Done (Tout compte fait, 1972), translated by Patrick O'Brian, G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York, 1974. Written sixty years after the event described here; the sentence continues in the source and is truncated at the semicolon of its argument
suggested_refs: The fifth-floor apartment on the rue de Rennes, sixth arrondissement, the family's address after 1919
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Institut Catholique de Paris, the certificates assembled
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sequence, dated loosely. She passes the baccalaureat in mathematics and philosophy in 1925 at seventeen, studies mathematics at the Institut Catholique in 1925-1926 and literature and languages at the Institut Sainte-Marie de Neuilly in 1926-1927, per French Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia. The month and day are defaulted to the start of an academic year. The Neuilly institute is a second site not given its own stop; Nominatim places it at 48.8852, 2.2813
stops.campa: She has no path, so she builds one out of pieces. At the Institut Catholique she reads mathematics; at the Institut Sainte-Marie de Neuilly, out in the western suburbs, she reads literature and languages; the certificates are collected one at a time toward a licence in philosophy that nobody in her family has asked her to want. Her father watches the assembly with a pride that is also an insult. He says of it, to anyone who will listen, that his daughter thinks like a man. She is still quoting the sentence to journalists in 1974.
stops.quote: Simone has a man's brain; she thinks like a man; she is a man.
stops.quote_source: Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, her father, on his daughter, relayed by Beauvoir in Caroline Moorehead, 'A talk with Simone de Beauvoir,' The New York Times, 2 June 1974, p. 258. Reported speech, not Beauvoir's own words
suggested_refs: The Institut Catholique de Paris, rue d'Assas
The Institut Sainte-Marie de Neuilly, boulevard Victor Hugo, Neuilly-sur-Seine
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'
Caroline Moorehead, 'A talk with Simone de Beauvoir,' The New York Times, 2 June 1974, p. 258 (paywalled, cited through Wikipedia's raw reference)

segments.name: The Sorbonne, the Pact, and the Death of Zaza

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the thesis on Leibniz
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929, corrected. The gathered chronology dated the Leibniz thesis to 1928; English Wikipedia gives the diplome work 'Le concept chez Leibniz' for Leon Brunschvicg as completed in 1929, and French Wikipedia gives her Sorbonne years as 1926-1928 with the diplome following in 1929. Month and day defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from claude_levi_strauss.journey.json, the atlas pin for the Sorbonne agregation track
stops.campa: For the diplome d'etudes superieures she writes on the concept in Leibniz, directed by Leon Brunschvicg, who has taught most of the philosophers France will be arguing with for the next forty years. The Sorbonne of these years admits women to its lecture halls and expects them to go and teach girls afterwards and stop there. The work is handed in in 1929, in the same season she is cramming for the agregation. She reads Leibniz on the individual notion that already contains everything that will ever happen to it.
suggested_refs: 'Le concept chez Leibniz', diplome d'etudes superieures directed by Leon Brunschvicg
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: The Sorbonne, second in France
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the ranking; July is given by the geography material and the day is defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from claude_levi_strauss.journey.json, whose own stop records Levi-Strauss passing the same concours in 1931, placed third
stops.campa: She sits the agregation de philosophie and places second in the country, behind Jean-Paul Sartre. She is twenty-one, the youngest person to have passed the examination at that date. They have been preparing for it together since the spring, and in October they will become a couple. From this July she may teach philosophy anywhere in France, which also means the ministry may post her anywhere in France it chooses, and it will. The rank converts into no chair and no laboratory, only a schoolmistress's salary and a railway ticket. Her first posting is the Lycee Victor-Duruy, in the autumn.
suggested_refs: The 1929 agregation de philosophie results, Sartre first and Beauvoir second
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: A bench outside the Louvre, the two-year lease
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the bench and the month's day. October 1929 for the beginning of the partnership is attested by English Wikipedia, which also carries the quoted line; the specific bench outside the Louvre comes from the memoir tradition and is not independently sited. Day defaulted
stops.campa: Sitting with Sartre on a bench outside the Louvre in October, she waits for the proposal a girl of her class is raised to expect, and gets a different offer instead. What he proposes instead is a contract. They are to be each other's essential love, free to take contingent ones, and obliged to tell each other everything, and the term is two years, renewable. It holds fifty-one years, through other beds, two wars and four continents. They never marry.
stops.quote_source: Jean-Paul Sartre to Beauvoir, October 1929, as quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Simone de Beauvoir'
suggested_refs: The essential love and contingent loves pact of October 1929
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Sceaux, the death of Elisabeth Lacoin
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected. The gathered chronology carried this as a reconstruction with no date; French Wikipedia's article on Elisabeth Lacoin gives it fully: born 25 December 1907 at Tours, died 25 November 1929 at Sceaux, aged twenty-one, of viral encephalitis, first symptoms 11 November, hospitalised 13 November, with Merleau-Ponty's proposal on 9 November
stops.campa: At Sceaux, on the twenty-fifth of November, Elisabeth Lacoin dies of viral encephalitis at twenty-one. She had fallen ill on the eleventh; Maurice Merleau-Ponty had proposed marriage to her on the ninth, and her family had been working against the match for months. Beauvoir refuses for the rest of her life to accept a virus as the whole account, and writes of the suffocating narrowness of a bourgeois patriarchal society that she believed had killed her friend. In the memoirs Zaza is given a false surname, Mabille, and the real one goes unprinted for decades.
suggested_refs: Elisabeth Lacoin's letters and diaries, published as Zaza: correspondance et carnets

stops.name: Lycee Victor-Duruy, the first post
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected. The gathered chronology said her teaching began at Marseille in 1931; French Wikipedia gives Lycee Victor-Duruy, Paris, 1929-1931 as the first post, and English Wikipedia states she taught at the lycee level from 1929 through 1943. Month defaulted to the start of the academic year. Coordinates corrected to Nominatim's for 33 boulevard des Invalides, 75007, about 460 m north of the gathered figure
stops.campa: Newly agregee, she is appointed to the Lycee Victor-Duruy on the boulevard des Invalides and teaches philosophy to girls in the seventh arrondissement for two years. She is twenty-one and her pupils are seventeen. She will teach at the lycee level in one city or another from 1929 until 1943, and publish her first book in the eleventh year of it. This is the shape the decade takes: a timetable, a chalk-dusted room, other people's daughters, and the writing done in cafes on either side of the school day.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Victor-Duruy, 33 boulevard des Invalides, her first teaching post

stops.name: Lycee Montgrand, Marseille
stops.date_confidence: attested to the academic year 1931-1932 by French Wikipedia; month defaulted. Coordinates corrected to Nominatim's for the Lycee Montgrand, 13 rue Montgrand, Marseille 6e, about 450 m from the gathered figure
stops.campa: Posted to the Lycee Montgrand on the rue Montgrand, she teaches philosophy alone in a provincial city for the first time, a long way from Sartre and from the circle that has been her whole intellectual weather since school. She answers the exile by walking: long solitary hikes into the hills behind the city, in a decade when a woman walking alone in open country is understood to be asking for whatever befalls her. The hills are the part she keeps writing about afterwards. She is there one academic year, 1931 to 1932.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Montgrand, 13 rue Montgrand, Marseille, her 1931-1932 post

stops.name: Lycee Jeanne-d'Arc, Rouen
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected. French Wikipedia gives Lycee Jeanne-d'Arc, Rouen, 1932-1936, not 1932-1937 as the gathered geography had it; she moves to the Lycee Moliere in Paris in 1936. Month defaulted. Coordinates corrected to Nominatim's for 2 rue du Mont, Rouen, about 670 m from the gathered figure. Olga Kosakiewicz is placed here rather than at the Lycee Moliere: English Wikipedia's article on her records her as Beauvoir's pupil at Rouen, introduced in 1932
stops.campa: Four years at the Lycee Jeanne-d'Arc on the rue du Mont, with the Paris train timetable learned by heart. In 1932 she is introduced to a pupil named Olga Kosakiewicz, and out of that introduction she and Sartre make a triangle that runs for years and ends in nobody's favour. The affair runs 1934 to 1935 with her and 1935 to 1937 with him. She takes the whole thing apart afterwards on paper and calls the result L'Invitee. Jacques-Laurent Bost, another of the Rouen students, becomes her lover and stays her friend for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Jeanne-d'Arc, 2 rue du Mont, Rouen
L'Invitee (1943), the novel made from the Rouen triangle
sources: Nominatim geocode, Lycee Jeanne d'Arc, Rouen

stops.name: Berlin, the Institut francais under the new regime
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded from the gathered tag. The 1934 Berlin visit rests on a single crawled characterisation; German Wikipedia's Beauvoir article records a Berlin trip in February 1948 and gives no 1934 trip at all. The gathered claim that she was observing 'Weimar-era culture in its final year' is impossible and is dropped: the Weimar Republic ended 23 March 1933. Month and day defaulted; coordinates are the city centre, no building located
stops.campa: She goes to Berlin to join Sartre, who has a year at the Institut francais reading Husserl. The city they walk in is not the Weimar city of the books they grew up on. The Republic has been dead for more than a year, the regime is a year into its work, and the phenomenology Sartre is importing into French philosophy is being read in a country busy expelling its philosophers. She notices the flags. What she writes about the trip at the time is mostly about Husserl, and the trip itself hangs on one thin thread of evidence.
suggested_refs: The Institut francais in Berlin, where Sartre held a research year
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Simone de Beauvoir' (attests a February 1948 Berlin trip, not a 1934 one)

stops.name: Lycee Moliere, the last classroom
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936-1939 by French Wikipedia; month defaulted. Coordinates corrected to Nominatim's for 71 rue du Ranelagh, 75016, about 490 m from the gathered figure. Bianca Bienenfeld, later Lamblin, is attested as her pupil here in 1937 by English Wikipedia; Natalie Sorokine likewise. Olga Kosakiewicz has been moved to the Rouen stop, where she belongs
stops.campa: Back in Paris at the Lycee Moliere on the rue du Ranelagh, teaching in the sixteenth arrondissement, still unpublished at twenty-eight. Two of her pupils here enter the private history that will later be used against her: Bianca Bienenfeld, whose teacher she is in 1937, and Natalie Sorokine. Both become her lovers, and both are passed on to Sartre. The classroom and the bedroom are not kept apart in this decade, and the separating gets done later, by other people, using the papers she left behind. In 1943 the ministry withdraws her licence to teach over the second of them, on conduct dated to 1939.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Moliere, 71 rue du Ranelagh, Paris 16e
Bianca Lamblin, Memoires d'une jeune fille derangee (Balland; English, A Disgraceful Affair)

stops.name: A Paris station, seeing Sartre off
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the station, corrected as to the framing. Sartre was mobilised and left on 2 September 1939; France declared war on Germany on 3 September, so the gathered phrase 'when France declares war' is wrong and is replaced by 'the day before'. Which of the Paris stations it was is not established in any source reached; the coordinates approximate the Gare de l'Est on the assumption of an eastern posting, and that assumption is the reconstruction
stops.campa: On the second of September, the day before France declares war, Sartre is mobilised and leaves Paris for the east. She goes with him to the station and comes back alone. For the next ten months she teaches, queues, writes, and waits for letters; the phoney war is her apprenticeship in the ordinary. The war diary she starts that autumn, published only after her death, records the day and the fear underneath it. Which station it was she does not say, and nobody has established it since.
suggested_refs: Journal de guerre, septembre 1939 - janvier 1941, published posthumously in 1990
sources: crawled dossier and general biographical consensus

stops.name: Cafe de Flore, the warm room
stops.date_confidence: attested for the association across 1940-1944; the year here is an ordering device inside that span and the month and day are defaulted. English Wikipedia's article on the Cafe de Flore documents the wartime circle at the cafe; the specific claim that Beauvoir wrote there daily is consistent with that source rather than verbatim from it
stops.campa: There is no coal. The Flore has a stove and a proprietor who does not mind how long a table is held, and so the upstairs room of the cafe on the boulevard Saint-Germain becomes the office in which two philosophers write their war. She arrives when it opens, takes the same table, writes until it closes, eats whatever there is. The Occupation makes a professional of her in a way the lycee never did: she has no money, no coal, and nothing else to do but work, and by 1943 she has a novel finished.
suggested_refs: The Cafe de Flore, 172 boulevard Saint-Germain, and its upstairs room

stops.name: Hotel La Louisiane, the room, the novel, and the licence
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, month and day defaulted. Corrected: the gathered chronology dated the Vichy investigation over Natalie Sorokine to 1941. English Wikipedia gives 1943 for the suspension from teaching, with the alleged conduct dated to 1939, and no source reached supports a 1941 investigation. The hotel room is attested from 1943 onward by French Wikipedia
stops.campa: She takes a room in the Hotel La Louisiane on the rue de Seine, one of the cheap Saint-Germain hotels the Left Bank writers are moving into and will not leave; she keeps a connection to it for years after she can afford otherwise. In the same year Gallimard publishes L'Invitee, her first novel, the Rouen triangle dismantled and reassembled as an ethics of jealousy. In the same year the ministry withdraws her licence to teach, on a complaint brought by Natalie Sorokine's mother, and her income after that is her writing. She is thirty-five.
suggested_refs: The Hotel La Louisiane, 60 rue de Seine, Saint-Germain-des-Pres

stops.name: Palais de Justice, the Brasillach trial
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1945 by English Wikipedia; the day is defaulted. Her essay 'Oeil pour oeil' is dated 1946 in the same source
stops.campa: At the Palais de Justice the collaborationist writer Robert Brasillach is tried for intelligence with the enemy and condemned to death. A petition for clemency circulates among the writers of Paris. Beauvoir will not sign it, and she goes to the courtroom to look at him. The essay she publishes the following year, Oeil pour oeil, argues that a man can place himself outside the human community by what he has done to it, and that the demand for his death is then not vengeance but the last available form of justice.
suggested_refs: 'Oeil pour oeil' (1946), her essay on the Brasillach case

stops.name: Gallimard, the founding of Les Temps Modernes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1945 by English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia; October is the month of the first number and the day is defaulted. Coordinates are Nominatim's for Editions Gallimard, 5 rue Gaston-Gallimard, 75007, formerly rue Sebastien-Bottin; the gathered afterlife lens had placed Gallimard 1.5 km away in the fifth arrondissement, which is wrong
stops.campa: With Sartre, Maurice Merleau-Ponty and others she founds Les Temps Modernes, a monthly with no owner but its editors and no line but the one they argue out among themselves. She sits on the committee from the first number and is still running the journal forty years later, when every one of the other founders is dead. Pyrrhus et Cineas, published the year before, had already set the question the journal exists to keep asking: what is a free man supposed to do about anybody else? The same year Gallimard brings out Le Sang des autres, the Resistance novel she wrote under the Occupation without knowing how it would end.
stops.quote: I wish that every human life might be pure transparent freedom.
stops.quote_source: The Blood of Others (Le Sang des autres, Gallimard, 1945; English translation by Yvonne Moyse and Roger Senhouse, 1948). Cited at book level: no page or chapter reference was reachable
suggested_refs: Les Temps Modernes, first number, October 1945
Pyrrhus et Cineas (1944)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'
Nominatim geocode, Editions Gallimard, 5 rue Gaston-Gallimard, 75007

stops.name: New York, the four-month tour begins
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1947 for the arrival and to four months for the tour, per the Stanford Encyclopedia and English Wikipedia's article on America Day by Day. Day defaulted; coordinates are a midtown Manhattan placement, not a specific address
stops.campa: She lands in the United States in January for a lecture tour of four months, carrying a suitcase of talks on existentialism and no clear idea what she is going to find. She writes in a diary every day of the trip, and the diary rather than the lectures is what survives, published the following year as L'Amerique au jour le jour. New York does not resemble a European city and she keeps saying so: the scale of it, the vertical light, the strangers who talk to her, the drugstores, the absence of any centre a walker can aim herself at.
suggested_refs: L'Amerique au jour le jour (1948), the travel diary of the tour
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Chicago, Nelson Algren's streets
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1947 for the meeting; month and day defaulted. Corrected on duration: the gathered chronology said the affair ran into the mid-1960s, but English Wikipedia's Algren article says the relationship had changed decisively by 1960, so it is given here as running through the 1950s with correspondence afterwards. The coordinates mark Algren's West Town neighbourhood, geocoded at 1958 West Evergreen Avenue, which was his last Chicago address from about 1959; his 1947 flat was on Wabansia Avenue and was not located
stops.campa: Nelson Algren meets her and takes her to the parts of Chicago the lecture circuit does not include: the bars, the police lineups, the rooming houses on the northwest side that he is writing his novels out of. She stays. What begins that week runs through the whole of the 1950s in letters across an ocean, and by 1960 has turned decisively into something else. The letters she writes him are published long after both of them are dead. He gives her a silver ring with Inca motifs on the morning after their first night together.
suggested_refs: Beauvoir's published letters to Nelson Algren
The silver ring with Inca motifs, worn to the grave
sources: Nominatim geocode, 1958 W Evergreen Avenue, Chicago

stops.name: San Francisco, the western end of the tour
stops.date_confidence: attested that San Francisco, Los Angeles, New Mexico, Texas, Georgia, Florida, New Orleans, Niagara and Virginia are all named stops on the 1947 itinerary, per English Wikipedia's article on America Day by Day. Corrected: that article gives no ordering and no arrival dates at all, so the gathered claim that the tour ended in New Orleans is dropped. Month and day here are an ordering device with no source behind them
stops.campa: The itinerary swings west and then south: Los Angeles, San Francisco, New Mexico, Texas, Georgia, Florida and New Orleans, with Niagara and the Virginia country behind her. Twelve states and four months, and a page written every night. What she puts down is a notebook, a European looking hard at the century's winner and finding it, inside the same paragraph, magnificent and unbearable. The order of the stops she never gives, and the book does not supply one either.
suggested_refs: The itinerary of the 1947 lecture tour as listed in America Day by Day

stops.name: Gallimard, an ethics of ambiguity and an American diary
stops.date_confidence: attested: Pour une morale de l'ambiguite in 1947, L'Amerique au jour le jour in 1948, per the Stanford Encyclopedia and English Wikipedia. The stop is dated to the later of the two; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Back in Paris she publishes Pour une morale de l'ambiguite, the fullest statement anybody in the existentialist circle makes of what an ethics without God would have to look like: freedom is not a possession but a task, and it is worth nothing at all if it is not also willed for everybody else. She is thirty-nine, she has published four books, and the French press still describes her as Sartre's companion. The American diary follows in 1948 as L'Amerique au jour le jour.
suggested_refs: Pour une morale de l'ambiguite (1947), The Ethics of Ambiguity
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Les Temps Modernes, the chapters serialised
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia carries the serialisation in Les Temps Modernes ahead of book publication, dated to mid-1949; the gathered chronology tagged it R and the tag is kept. Day defaulted. Coordinates are the Gallimard pin, the journal's publisher and address
stops.campa: Chapters of the book she has been calling an essay on the condition of women start appearing in Les Temps Modernes ahead of the volumes, in the middle of 1949, in the journal she helped found and still edits. The answer comes back at once and it is not literary: letters, insults, reviews written by men who have read the extracts on sexual initiation and nothing else in it. She goes on serialising. The full work is already at the printer, and the printer is Gallimard.
stops.quote: One is not born a genius, one becomes a genius; and the feminine situation has up to the present rendered this becoming practically impossible.
stops.quote_source: The Second Sex, Book I, Part 2, Chapter 8, p. 133, H. M. Parshley translation
suggested_refs: The 1949 Les Temps Modernes instalments preceding Le Deuxieme Sexe

stops.name: Gallimard, Le Deuxieme Sexe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949 for publication in two volumes by Gallimard, 978 pages, and for the placing on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum until the Index was abolished in 1966, per English Wikipedia's article on The Second Sex. Month and day are an ordering device. Corrected: the November 2009 unabridged English translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier was published by Jonathan Cape in the United Kingdom, with the Knopf edition following in 2010
stops.campa: Gallimard publishes Le Deuxieme Sexe in two volumes, Les faits et les mythes and L'experience vecue, nine hundred and seventy-eight pages, and the argument inside them is that womanhood is not a nature but a construction, made daily, by a world that afterwards calls the result destiny. The first English translation, made by a zoologist and cut by roughly a third, is the version most of the anglophone twentieth century reads. The Vatican puts the book on the Index of prohibited books, where it stays until the Index itself is abolished in 1966.
stops.quote: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
stops.quote_source: The Second Sex (Le Deuxieme Sexe, 1949), Book 2, Part 4, Chapter 1, 'Childhood'; H. M. Parshley translation, p. 267
suggested_refs: The 1953 H. M. Parshley translation for Alfred A. Knopf, abridged
The 2009 Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier translation, Jonathan Cape, unabridged

stops.name: Paris, Les Mandarins and the Goncourt
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1954 for the novel and the Prix Goncourt, and to 1952 for the beginning of her life with Claude Lanzmann, per English Wikipedia. Month and day are an ordering device. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin shared across the atlas
stops.campa: Les Mandarins takes the Prix Goncourt: a novel about the Paris intellectuals of the Liberation, their journal, their quarrel over the camps in the East, and a woman's affair with an American writer in Chicago. It is dedicated to Nelson Algren. The Goncourt makes her at forty-six a public figure in her own name, five years after Le Deuxieme Sexe and on the strength of a novel. Since 1952 she has been living with Claude Lanzmann, seventeen years her junior, in Montparnasse.
suggested_refs: Les Mandarins (1954), Prix Goncourt, dedicated to Nelson Algren

stops.name: 11 bis rue Victor-Schoelcher, the last address
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955-1986 by French Wikipedia; month and day defaulted. Coordinates corrected to Nominatim's for 11 bis rue Victor Schoelcher, 75014, about 320 m from the gathered figure
stops.campa: She is forty-seven when she takes a studio at 11 bis rue Victor-Schoelcher in the fourteenth arrondissement, one room and a mezzanine, looking onto the wall of the Montparnasse cemetery, and she lives here for the last thirty-one years of her life, from 1955 to 1986. The room fills up over the decades with what she carries back from the trips, objects out of Havana and Peking and Cairo, and with manuscripts stacked on the floor where the shelves have run out.
suggested_refs: The studio at 11 bis rue Victor-Schoelcher, Paris 14e, her home 1955-1986
sources: Nominatim geocode, 11 bis rue Victor Schoelcher, 75014

stops.name: Beijing, the long march looked at
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955 for the China trip, corroborated by English Wikipedia and a surviving photograph of the pair in Beijing; the month is an ordering device with no source behind it and the day is defaulted. The atlas file mao_zedong.journey.json has no 1955 stop, its dated stops running 1945-1950, so this crossing sits outside that file's covered years
stops.campa: She and Sartre travel to the People's Republic as guests of a state six years old. She is shown factories, communes, schools and the new marriage law, and what she carries away is the claim that a revolution has undone in ten years a subjection Europe has not touched in a century. La Longue Marche, the book she makes out of the trip, is a sympathetic account of Mao Zedong's revolution written by a visitor who was shown what her hosts intended her to see. A photograph survives of the two of them in Peking.
suggested_refs: La Longue Marche (1957), her book on the Chinese revolution
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Gallimard, La Longue Marche and the Memoires
stops.date_confidence: attested: La Longue Marche 1957, Memoires d'une jeune fille rangee 1958, per English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia. The stop is dated to the earlier of the two; month and day defaulted. The quoted sentence is confirmed verbatim from Wikipedia's raw wikitext, which cites only 'Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter, Book One'; the page number 41 that circulates with it is not in the source and is dropped
stops.campa: La Longue Marche appears in 1957. The year after it she publishes Memoires d'une jeune fille rangee and finds, at fifty, the form she will spend the rest of her working life in: her own life told straight, with the names changed where the living would be hurt by them. The first volume ends with Zaza dead at Sceaux. It sells as no philosophy of hers has ever sold, and the letters that come back are overwhelmingly from women. Three more volumes follow.
stops.quote: ...my father's individualism and pagan ethical standards were in complete contrast to the rigidly moral conventionalism of my mother's teaching.
stops.quote_source: Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter (Memoires d'une jeune fille rangee, 1958), Book One. Cited at book level: the page number sometimes given with this line is not in Wikipedia's underlying reference

stops.name: Havana, the photograph with Guevara
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded from the gathered tag. English Wikipedia's Beauvoir article captions a photograph 'Antonio Nunez Jimenez, Beauvoir, Sartre and Che Guevara in Cuba, 1960' but gives no month; English Wikipedia's Sartre article says only that he went to Cuba 'in the 1960s' to meet Castro and spoke with Guevara, with no year. The month here is an ordering device. che_guevara.journey.json has a Havana stop dated 1960-03-05 for Korda's photograph at the La Coubre funeral; same trip is plausible, same day is not established
stops.campa: In Cuba, a year into the revolution, she and Sartre are received by a government of men in their thirties. A photograph is taken of the two of them with Ernesto Che Guevara and Antonio Nunez Jimenez, four people at a table. She writes about the island afterwards in the register she had used for Peking five years before. Sartre's own record of the journey says only that he went to Cuba to meet Fidel Castro and spoke with Guevara. What month she was there, and what was said at that table, is in no record that has been reached.
suggested_refs: The 1960 photograph of Nunez Jimenez, Beauvoir, Sartre and Guevara in Cuba

stops.name: Paris, the Djamila Boupacha campaign
stops.date_confidence: attested. Beauvoir's Le Monde article of 2 June 1960 and the seizure of copies in Algiers are given by English Wikipedia's article on Djamila Boupacha; the book with Gisele Halimi is 1962. Corrected: the gathered chronology welded the 1962 book to the Manifesto of the 343, which is April 1971, and the two have been separated. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin, a general locus; the 1960 offices of Le Monde were not located
stops.campa: Djamila Boupacha of the Algerian FLN is arrested, tortured and raped in French custody, and Beauvoir puts the fact on the front page of Le Monde on the second of June. Copies of the paper are seized and destroyed in Algiers. With the lawyer Gisele Halimi she assembles a defence committee and, two years later, a book that carries the case in documents. She has been publishing against the war in Les Temps Modernes since 1955, when supporting Algerian independence still cost a French writer readers.
stops.quote: All oppression creates a state of war.
stops.quote_source: The Second Sex (1949), Conclusion, p. 717, H. M. Parshley translation
suggested_refs: Simone de Beauvoir and Gisele Halimi, Djamila Boupacha (Gallimard, 1962)

stops.name: Paris, a very easy death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1964 for publication by English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia; month and day defaulted. Coordinates are the Gallimard pin. The clinical detail of the mother's last illness comes from the book itself and was not independently re-verified
stops.campa: Her mother dies of cancer after a fall, six weeks in a bed, and Beauvoir writes it down: the surgeons who will not say the word, the daughters who agree not to say it either, the body that becomes an object of care and then simply an object. Une mort tres douce is short and contains no philosophy at all. She had spent her adult life refusing everything her mother stood for, and the book takes none of that back. It only stays in the room. She is fifty-six years old.
suggested_refs: Une mort tres douce (1964), A Very Easy Death
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Cairo, at Nasser's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1967 by the photograph caption on English Wikipedia's Jean-Paul Sartre article, which names Sartre, Beauvoir and Claude Lanzmann meeting President Nasser at his home in Cairo. Day defaulted. The purpose of the trip, a special number of Les Temps Modernes on the Arab-Israeli conflict, is carried from the gathered material and was not independently re-fetched
stops.campa: Beauvoir, Sartre and Claude Lanzmann are received by Gamal Abdel Nasser at his house in Cairo in February. They have come to gather material for a special number of Les Temps Modernes on the Arab-Israeli conflict, in which both sides are to be given their own writers and their own pages and no editorial verdict is to be handed down. The issue appears in the spring. In June the war starts. The number sells out, and the position it took holds for about three weeks.
suggested_refs: The 1967 Les Temps Modernes special number on the Arab-Israeli conflict

stops.name: Tel Aviv, received by Levi Eshkol
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, genuinely uncertain. The claim rests on a Wikimedia Commons caption attributed to the Israeli Government Press Office and nothing else; the Levi Eshkol article makes no mention of Beauvoir, and no news source could be reached. The Cairo leg of the same trip is well attested, which makes an Israel leg plausible but does not establish it. Note also that the interlock pass found no other atlas traveller with a Cairo, Tel Aviv or Jerusalem stop in this period
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of March, at the other end of the same journey, she is said to have been received in Tel Aviv by the Israeli prime minister Levi Eshkol. The claim rests on a captioned photograph credited to a government press office and on nothing else that could be reached; Eshkol's own record does not mention her. She was certainly in the region that season, and certainly in Cairo. Whether she sat in that room is a thing the sources assert and do not show.
suggested_refs: The Israeli Government Press Office photograph said to show Beauvoir with Levi Eshkol, 29 March 1967

stops.name: Gallimard, La Vieillesse
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1970 by English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia; month and day defaulted. Quotations confirmed with part, chapter and page from the cited Wikiquote entry
stops.campa: La Vieillesse does to the aged what Le Deuxieme Sexe had done to women: it takes a condition presented as nature and shows it to be something a society makes and then declines to look at. At sixty-two she is writing about a category she has herself only just entered, and the English edition will be called The Coming of Age. She reads the ethnographers, the demographers, the pension figures and the poets, and reports what the old are paid, where they are put, and how long they are left there.
stops.quote: Society cares about the individual only in so far as he is profitable.
stops.quote_source: The Coming of Age (La Vieillesse, 1970), Conclusion, p. 543
suggested_refs: La Vieillesse (1970), The Coming of Age
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: Le Nouvel Observateur, the Manifesto of the 343
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1971 by French and English Wikipedia; day defaulted. Corrected: the gathered chronology dated this to 1962 alongside the Djamila Boupacha book, nine years early, and the two have been separated. Coordinates are an approximate central Paris placement for the magazine's offices in this period, not verified against any address record
stops.campa: Three hundred and forty-three women put their names in Le Nouvel Observateur under a declaration that they have had abortions, which is at that date a crime in France carrying prison. Beauvoir drafts the text and signs it, alongside actresses, writers, and women nobody has heard of. The signature of the author of Le Deuxieme Sexe is the one that makes the list impossible to prosecute. Not one of the three hundred and forty-three is ever charged. Four years later the Veil law passes.
suggested_refs: The Manifeste des 343, Le Nouvel Observateur, April 1971

stops.name: Paris, the word said about herself
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1972 for the Le Nouvel Observateur interview declaring herself a feminist. Corrected: English Wikipedia dates the founding of Questions feministes to 1972 as well, and that is an error; French Wikipedia states she took the editorial direction of the journal at its creation in 1977, which the journal's own publication record supports. Month and day defaulted. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: In an interview with Le Nouvel Observateur she says the word about herself for the first time: she is a feminist. In Le Deuxieme Sexe, twenty-three years before, she had held that the liberation of women would follow from socialism and needed no separate movement of its own. She has changed her mind, publicly, in a magazine, at sixty-four, and she says so in exactly those terms. In 1977 she takes the editorial direction of the journal Questions feministes.
stops.quote: I tore myself away from the safe comfort of certainties through my love for truth—and truth rewarded me.
stops.quote_source: All Said and Done (Tout compte fait, 1972), p. 16. Verbatim, including the source's own dash
suggested_refs: The 1972 Le Nouvel Observateur interview
Questions feministes, founded 1977

stops.name: Paris, the interview with Betty Friedan
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's raw wikitext gives the citation as 'Sex, Society, and the Female Dilemma', interview with Betty Friedan, The Saturday Review, pp. 12-21, 14 June 1975. Corrected: the widely circulated continuation of the quotation, about too many women making that choice, is not at that citation and could not be traced to the Saturday Review text or anywhere else, so only the two verifiable sentences are carried
stops.campa: Betty Friedan comes to Paris to interview her for an American magazine, and the conversation goes wrong in a way both of them find useful. Friedan wants choice: a woman may take a job or may keep a house, whichever she prefers, and the movement ought to defend either. Beauvoir refuses the premise outright, in two sentences that are still being quoted against her fifty years afterwards. The interview runs in The Saturday Review in June under the title Sex, Society, and the Female Dilemma.
stops.quote: No, we don't believe that any woman should have this choice. No woman should be authorized to stay at home and raise her children.
stops.quote_source: 'Sex, Society, and the Female Dilemma', interview with Betty Friedan, The Saturday Review, 14 June 1975, pp. 12-21
suggested_refs: 'Sex, Society, and the Female Dilemma', The Saturday Review, 14 June 1975
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Simone de Beauvoir' (raw wikitext reference)

stops.name: Paris, the manifesto against repression in Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1977 by Italian Wikipedia's record of the Manifesto contro la repressione, signed by twenty-eight intellectuals including Sartre, Beauvoir, Foucault, Barthes, Deleuze and Guattari; the day is defaulted. Coordinates and date inherited byte-identical from felix_guattari.journey.json, which carries the same event as an attested stop
stops.campa: Twenty-eight French intellectuals sign an appeal against the Italian crackdown that followed the killing of the student Francesco Lorusso in Bologna. She is sixty-nine, and has been putting her name to lists for thirty years on the calculation that a name worth something is only worth anything spent. The generation signing beside her here was in the lycee when Le Deuxieme Sexe came out. Beauvoir signs and Sartre signs; Michel Foucault and Roland Barthes sign; Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari sign.

stops.name: Paris, the petition of 1977
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1977 by English Wikipedia; month and day defaulted, and the ordering against the July manifesto is therefore arbitrary. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: She signs a petition asking for the release of three men convicted of sexual acts with minors. It belongs to a campaign in the French press of those years, joined by a large part of the Paris intelligentsia, to abolish or lower the age of consent. The petition is a matter of record and her name is on it. It sits in the same year as the manifesto against repression in Italy and five years after she called herself a feminist in a magazine, and nobody, including her, has ever explained it away.
suggested_refs: The 1977 French petitions on the age of consent and their signatories

stops.name: Paris, the adoption of Sylvie Le Bon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1980 for the adoption; month and day defaulted. Corrected: the gathered chronology described them as intimate since the 1960s, which is not attested and which Le Bon has publicly disputed. English Wikipedia's article on Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir says they met in 1960, when Le Bon was nineteen and Beauvoir fifty-two, and that the 1980 adoption made her sole executor. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: She legally adopts Sylvie Le Bon, whom she met in 1960 when Le Bon was nineteen and she was fifty-two, a philosophy student who has become the closest person to her. The adoption makes Le Bon her sole heir and literary executor, which is what it is for: French law offers an unmarried woman no other way to leave her papers to the person she chooses. Le Bon will spend the following four decades editing and publishing them, volume by volume, the letters and the diaries and the war journals alike.
suggested_refs: The posthumous editions of Beauvoir's letters and diaries edited by Sylvie Le Bon-de Beauvoir

stops.name: Boulevard du Montparnasse, Sartre's cortege
stops.date_confidence: attested. Sartre died of pulmonary oedema on 15 April 1980; the funeral of 19 April and the crowd of fifty thousand are given by English Wikipedia's Jean-Paul Sartre article. The detail of Beauvoir being sedated is her own account in La Ceremonie des adieux and was not independently re-verified
stops.campa: Sartre dies of pulmonary oedema on the fifteenth of April, seventy-four years old, ending fifty-one years of a contract signed on a bench outside the Louvre. Beauvoir, by her own account in La Ceremonie des adieux, is sedated at the hospital and taken away from the body she had asked to lie down beside. On the nineteenth, fifty thousand people fill the boulevard du Montparnasse behind the coffin, unorganised and unannounced by any party, walking toward a cemetery a few hundred metres from her own front door.

stops.name: Gallimard, La Ceremonie des adieux and the ribbon refused
stops.date_confidence: attested: La Ceremonie des adieux 1981, the refusal of the Legion of Honour offered by Francois Mitterrand's government 1982, per English Wikipedia and the Stanford Encyclopedia. The stop is dated to the earlier of the two; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: La Ceremonie des adieux is the account of Sartre's last ten years: the failing sight, the failing body, the young disciples around the chair, the mind going out. She publishes it while nearly everyone in it is still alive, and is attacked for it by people who had spent thirty years describing her as his shadow. It is a report, written in the same flat clinical prose she had used for her mother's dying. The following year the government of Francois Mitterrand offers her the Legion of Honour. She declines it.
stops.quote: Self-knowledge is no guarantee of happiness, but it is on the side of happiness and can supply the courage to fight for it.
stops.quote_source: Force of Circumstance (La Force des choses, Gallimard, 1963), the third volume of her memoirs, translated by Richard Howard, 1968. Cited at book level; no page reference was reachable
suggested_refs: La Ceremonie des adieux (1981), Adieux: A Farewell to Sartre
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simone de Beauvoir'

stops.name: 11 bis rue Victor-Schoelcher, the fourteenth of April
stops.date_confidence: date, cause and age attested: pneumonia, 14 April 1986, aged seventy-eight, per English Wikipedia. The place is contested and is NOT resolved here: French and Spanish Wikipedia both put the death at 11 bis rue Victor-Schoelcher, Spanish adding that she was accompanied by her adopted daughter and Claude Lanzmann, while English-language obituaries put it at the Hopital Cochin, whose own coordinates are 48.8370, 2.3402. The pin follows the French and Spanish record; the conflict stands open. Corrected: she did not die six years to the day after Sartre, who died 15 April 1980
stops.campa: She dies on the fourteenth of April, of pneumonia, at seventy-eight, one day short of six years after Sartre. The French and Spanish records put the death in the studio on the rue Victor-Schoelcher, with Sylvie Le Bon and Claude Lanzmann in the room; the English obituaries put it at the Hopital Cochin, twenty minutes' walk to the east. Nobody has reconciled the two accounts. She had lived in the one room for thirty-one years and had been working in it until the illness.
suggested_refs: The obituaries of April 1986 in The Guardian and the Los Angeles Times, which give the Hopital Cochin

stops.campa: They bury her in division 20 of the Montparnasse cemetery, just inside the gate on the boulevard Edgar-Quinet, in Sartre's grave. On her finger is the silver ring with Inca motifs that Nelson Algren gave her in Chicago in 1947, the morning after their first night. Some five thousand people come, most of them women, walking the same boulevard the fifty thousand had walked six years before. The stone carries two names and four dates and no epitaph of any kind.
